# Published hard-to-round inputs for asin, one double per line as its raw bits in hex
# (Double.doubleToRawLongBits), read by Inputs.hardCases("asin"). Lines starting with # are
# comments. Only the input values are taken from the source below; they are numeric facts.
#
# At such an input the exact asin(x) lies unusually close to a rounding boundary of binary64
# (a midpoint between two doubles for round-to-nearest, a double itself for the directed
# modes), so an implementation's last few rounding errors decide which double it returns. For a
# port that follows fdlibm's operations exactly they are no harder than any other input; their
# use here is that a dropped correction term or a reassociated sum, a change far below one ulp,
# is most likely to flip the result exactly at these points.
#
# Section 1: V. Lefevre, hard-to-round cases in round-to-nearest, file testlibm-data (updated
# 2020-11-27), https://www.vinc17.net/research/testlibm/testlibm-data.xz, from the page
# https://www.vinc17.net/research/testlibm/, which states no licence or reuse terms. Every
# line for "asn" in mode N, in the file's order, written by dev/testlibm-extract.py (python3 -I
# dev/testlibm-extract.py asn asin testlibm-data.xz), which rechecks each line with 400-digit
# decimal arithmetic (Python's decimal module: a Taylor series of atan after halving the angle,
# pi from Machin's formula, and asin(x) as atan(x / sqrt(1 - x^2))) before printing it: every
# input is a double, the file's result is asin(x) rounded to nearest, and the file's direction
# bit is the 54th bit of the exact asin(x). Measured by the same run: of these 1655 inputs all
# but one have at least 40 bits after the round bit pointing at the midpoint (the fewest is 1
# bit). All are positive and between 6.5e-8 and 1: asin is odd, and the tests also draw the
# negated inputs. The input 1.0 (0x3ff0000000000000) is one of them, and the port finishes it
# per lane, as every lane of 1 or more in magnitude.
